verses.text: After saying goodbye, we set sail straight for Cos. The next day we reached Rhodes, and from there we went to Patara.
There we found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, so we boarded and sailed on.
When Cyprus came into view, we passed it on our left and sailed to Syria. We landed at Tyre, where the ship had to unload its cargo.
We found some disciples there and stayed seven days. Through the Spirit, they urged Paul not to go to Jerusalem.
When our time there was up, we continued the journey. All the disciples, with their wives and children, walked with us outside the city. On the beach we knelt and prayed.
After saying goodbye, we boarded the ship, and they went back home.
We completed the voyage from Tyre and arrived in Ptolemais. We greeted the believers there and stayed with them for one day.
The next day we left for Caesarea with Paul’s companions. We stayed at the home of Philip the evangelist, one of the Seven.
Philip had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
We had been there several days when a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul’s belt, tied up his own hands and feet, and said, “The Holy Spirit says: ‘This is how the Jews in Jerusalem will tie up the man who owns this belt and hand him over to the Gentiles.’”
When we heard this, we and the local believers begged Paul not to go to Jerusalem.
Then Paul replied, “Why are you crying and breaking my heart? I’m ready not only to be tied up in Jerusalem but even to die there for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
When he wouldn’t be persuaded, we gave up and said, “May the Lord’s will be done.”
After those days, we packed our things and went up to Jerusalem.
Some disciples from Caesarea came with us. They brought us to Mnason, a disciple from Cyprus from the early days, whose home would host us.
When we reached Jerusalem, the believers welcomed us warmly.
The next day Paul went with us to see James. All the elders were there.
Paul greeted them and gave a detailed report of everything God had done among the Gentiles through his work.
When they heard it, they praised God. Then they said, “Brother, you can see how many thousands of Jews have believed, and they’re all deeply committed to the Law.
“But they’ve heard rumors about you—that you tell Jews living among the Gentiles to turn away from Moses, and tell them not to circumcise their children or follow our customs.
“So what should we do? They’ll surely hear that you’ve arrived, and the church will meet.
“Here’s what we want you to do. We have four men who have made a vow.

“Go with them and take part in the purification ritual. Pay their expenses so they can shave their heads. Then everyone will know there’s nothing to those rumors about you and that you also live in line with the Law.
“As for Gentile believers, we’ve already sent them our decision: they should avoid food offered to idols, blood, meat from strangled animals, and sexual immorality.”

So Paul took the men with him. The next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple to announce when the purification days would be completed and the offering made for each of them.
The seven days were almost over when some Jews from Asia saw Paul in the temple. They stirred up the whole crowd and grabbed him,

shouting, “People of Israel, help us! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against our people, the Law, and this place! He even brought Greeks into the temple and made this holy place unclean!”
They had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with Paul in the city and assumed Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city erupted. People rushed together, seized Paul, and dragged him out of the temple. The gates were shut at once.
They were trying to kill him when word reached the Roman commander that all Jerusalem was in an uproar.
He immediately took soldiers and officers and ran down to the crowd. When the people saw the commander and soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
The commander came up, arrested Paul, and ordered him bound with two chains. Then he asked who he was and what he had done.
Some people in the crowd shouted one thing, others something else. The commander couldn’t get a clear answer because of all the noise, so he ordered Paul taken to the barracks.
When Paul reached the stairs, the soldiers had to carry him because the crowd was so violent.
The crowd followed, shouting, “Get rid of him!”
As Paul was being taken into the barracks, he asked the commander, “May I say something to you?” The commander replied, “You speak Greek?
“Aren’t you the Egyptian who recently started a revolt and led four thousand members of the Assassins out into the wilderness?”
Paul said, “I’m a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of a well-known city. Please let me speak to the people.”
The commander gave him permission. Paul stood on the stairs, motioned to the crowd, and when everything had gone quiet, he addressed them in Hebrew:
